name: Kuku Yalanji, Muluriji dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Patz, Elisabeth. 2002. A grammar of the Kuku Yalanji language of north Queensland. Pacific Linguistics 527. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, ANU. Open PDF, sealang.net Pacific Linguistics archive (http://sealang.net/archives/pl/pdf/PL-527.pdf).
catalog_locator: sec. 2.6 'Stress and intonation' and 2.6.1 'Word stress', pp.35-36; sec. 2.6.2 'Clause stress' pp.36-37; sec. 1.1.2 pp.3-6 (Muluriji = dialect no.6 of Kuku Yalanji, Table 1.1 p.5 / Map 2 p.4; p.6 applicability sentence); sec. 2.3(iv) p.29 loan epenthesis; sec. 3.2.3.7(iii) p.60 mala- stems
catalog_quote: Every word in Kuku Yalanji has primary stress on the first syllable, after which there is a distinct drop in pitch for disyllabic words and a more gradual drop for words of more than two syllables (see Hershberger & Pike 1970:791-792). Words with four or more syllables that are roots, reduplicated forms, or compounds, may have secondary stress on the third syllable, that is the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated forms of compounds. A reduplicated trisyllabic root may have secondary stress on the fourth syllable, again the first syllable of the second root. ... However, secondary stress is not obligatory and is usually omitted in other than careful citation forms, leaving the word with stress only on the first syllable. ... But again, secondary stress is not obligatory and is in fact apparent only in slow and careful speech. In normal speech, even in long words of up to eight syllables, only the first syllable is stressed, with pitch subsiding over the following two or three syllables and remaining level over the rest. [p.6] Because of the attested close similarity between the dialects of Kuku Yalanji, the linguistic details described here may be taken to apply to the Kuku Yalanji language.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the first syllable of every word (stress = higher pitch and loudness); clause stress also falls on a word-initial syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional, careful/slow speech only: on the first syllable of the second root in reduplications and compounds (3rd or 4th syllable); disyllabic suffixes may take secondary stress on their first syllable; with monosyllabic suffixes/clitics, a word of more than three syllables takes secondary stress on the penult unless that is the last root syllable. In normal speech even words of up to eight syllables have only the initial stress, pitch subsiding over the next two or three syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: The adjective sequence -baja-ku 'very' is never stressed (yalbay-baja-ku), contra Hershberger & Pike who treat bajaku as a word; epenthetic vowels breaking loanword initial clusters are stressed by the normal rule (p.31).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for all words including inflected forms with clitics; secondary stresses described for careful citation forms; clause stress (sec. 2.6.2) coincides with word-initial stress of the focused constituent. Data are from eastern Yalanji and Kuku Nyungkul speakers; applied to Muluriji only via the author's statement that the description holds for the Kuku Yalanji language and its closely similar dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: No Muluridyi-specific description exists: the variety is known only from c. 450 words of field vocabulary (Hale c.1960 from Johnnie Diamond and Millie Martin; Dixon 1960s-70s from Nicholas Satani and Jack Cummings; Dixon 1970:675, Dixon 1982 'only a few hundred words have been recorded'; AUSTLANG Y97 grammar/wordlist/dictionary scores all 0). Patz 2002 (following Patz 1982, adopted by AUSTLANG, Glottolog and Dixon 2002) classifies Muluriji as one of ~13 dialects of the Kuku Yalanji language (kuku1273 = Glottolog's Kuku-Yalanji) and states that her description, based on eastern Yalanji and Kuku Nyungkul data, 'may be taken to apply to the Kuku Yalanji language' as a whole. The quoted stress statement is therefore first-hand for Kuku Yalanji (eastern Yalanji/Nyungkul speakers, Bloomfield River / Wujal Wujal) and applies to Muluridyi only by dialect membership; it should be catalogued with that flag (same statement as Hershberger & Pike 1970 for eastern Gugu-Yalanji, already held under kuku1273).

new_statements.relation_note: Verbatim identical to the Patz 2002 sec. 2.6.1 statement already in existing_statements; this thesis is the original source of that grammar. Confirms fixed initial stress. On dialect coverage: the thesis describes eastern Yalanji and Nyungkul (p. 8); Muluriji is dialect no. 6 in Map 2 (p. 4) and Table 1.1 (p. 6; Tindale 'Muluridji', Dixon 'Muluridyi'); p. 6 notes 'the data for Kuku Tyunkay is in fact identical to that for Muluridyi'; p. 8: 'Because of the attested close similarity between the dialects of Kuku Yalanji, the linguistic details described here may be taken to apply to the "Kuku Yalanji language"'. Quote checked against the page scan of p. 61.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is always on the first syllable of every word; stress is realised by higher pitch and loudness. Secondary stress is optional and appears only in slow, careful citation forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional, careful-speech only: on the 3rd syllable of 4+-syllable roots, reduplications and compounds (the first syllable of the second root; 4th syllable for reduplicated trisyllabic roots); on the first syllable of disyllabic inflections or derivational suffixes; with monosyllabic suffixes/clitics, on the penultimate syllable of words of more than three syllables unless that syllable is the last root syllable (pp. 62-63). In normal speech only the first syllable is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: The suffix+clitic sequence -baja-ku attached to an adjective never carries stress (contra Hershberger/Pike's treatment of bajaku as a word), p. 63. No exception to initial primary stress is given.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Muluriji itself; all stress evidence is for eastern Kuku Yalanji (Bloomfield River) and Nyungkul. Patz 1982 pp. 4-8 lists Muluriji (Muluridyi/Muluridji) as one of thirteen attested Kuku Yalanji dialects sharing 70-90%+ vocabulary with close morphological agreement, and states that the description may be taken to apply to the Kuku Yalanji language as a whole; the catalog's entry for mulu1243 rests on that extrapolation. Work 0 concerns Mbabaram (mbab1239), an unrelated Paman language.
